tribulation

trib-yoo-LAY-shun · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Tribulation is great trouble or suffering endured over a long period; a severe, drawn-out trial.

The family's years of tribulation after the flood -- lost jobs, a lost home, months in temporary shelters -- finally ended when they moved into a new apartment.

Example

Despite the tribulation of losing three crops in a row to drought, the farmers refused to sell the land that had been in their family for generations.

Tribulation describes serious, often prolonged suffering -- not a minor annoyance, but a genuine ordeal.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

ordeal: An ordeal is one severe, harrowing experience -- it can be over in a day or even an hour. A tribulation is suffering that stretches on: a whole season of trouble rather than a single trial. One brutal exam is an ordeal; a year of them is tribulation.

hardship: Hardship is severe difficulty in the conditions someone lives under -- poverty, hunger, punishing weather. A tribulation is the suffering itself, endured over a long time: hardship describes what your circumstances are, while tribulation describes the drawn-out trial of living through them.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

comfort: a state of ease, free from suffering

prosperity: a state of flourishing success and good fortune

Where it sits · how heavy the hardship is — inconvenience → tribulation → anguish

inconvenience vs. tribulation: An inconvenience is a minor annoyance or difficulty, far milder than a tribulation.

anguish vs. tribulation: Anguish is severe mental or physical suffering, even more intense than tribulation.

Build the Word

The pieces

root (historical) — tribul-

root (historical) — tribul-: from Latin tribulum, a heavy threshing tool once dragged over grain to separate it from the husk -- tribulation borrows that image of being 'ground down' (Latin)

suffix — -ation

suffix — -ation: the act, process, or result of (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Tribulation comes from Latin tribulum, a threshing tool dragged over harvested grain to separate it from the husk. To undergo tribulation is to feel 'ground down' the way that tool ground down grain.

Use the root in a new word: tribulate (a rare, old verb)

Use the root in a new word: tribulate (a rare, old verb): Tribulation comes from Latin tribulum, the name of a heavy board farmers dragged over harvested grain to crush the husks loose. Older texts sometimes used a matching verb, 'to tribulate,' though only the noun form survived into everyday English.

Word Building

Word Choice

Tribulation describes serious, often prolonged suffering -- not a minor inconvenience. It's frequently used in the plural, 'tribulations,' and often paired with 'trials,' as in 'trials and tribulations.'
